t: NASA’s Northrop Grumman CRS-25 Mission Overview

p: NASA’s Northrop Grumman Commercial Resupply Services 25 mission, or Northrop Grumman CRS-25, will deliver about 11,000 pounds of science and supplies to the International Space Station. The mission will be the third flight of the company’s Cygnus XL, the larger, more cargo-capable version of the company’s solar-powered spacecraft.

The Cygnus XL will launch aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Following arrival to the station, astronauts aboard the space station will use the Canadarm2 to grapple the spacecraft before ground controllers robotically install it to the Unity module’s Earth-facing port for cargo unloading.

uses the microgravity environment to explore potential treatments for muscle loss. Muscle atrophy and strength loss experienced by astronauts after spaceflight share many features with age-related muscle decline on Earth and occur more rapidly in microgravity without exercise. Researchers will use a muscle tissue model to test different Food and Drug Administration-approved drugs used to treat other conditions can be repurposed to prevent or reduce muscle loss.

Credit: University of Connecticut The

investigation uses microgravity to manufacture tiny, DNA-inspired particles designed to deliver medicine into dense tissues, such as cartilage and solid tumors. Microgravity may enable more uniform particle assembly, helping researchers refine production methods. The results could advance targeted treatments for cancer and osteoarthritis on Earth.

) will test a small radiation monitoring device to support future Artemis program and lunar missions. The system is designed to integrate with spacecraft systems and provide real-time radiation monitoring inside crew living areas. The results could inform radiation monitoring strategies and crew safety measures for future exploration missions.

uses miniature replicas of patients’ tumors to study how cancer cells move, invade surrounding tissues, and potentially spread. Researchers aim to develop a space-based diagnostic tool that could predict cancer progression months or even years in advance, improving early detection and treatment decisions for patients on Earth.

is a new plant growth facility designed to help food crop production on future long-duration missions. The mostly automated system uses innovative water recovery and air exchange technologies to grow a variety of crops. This research could help lead to better food production methods to keep crew healthy and fed on future exploration missions, including those to Mars.

img.cap: The upcoming JOINS demonstration inside the Bishop Airlock will perform autonomous robotic welding in space. JOINS will test two distinct approaches: laser beam welding and friction stir welding. Laser beam welding uses a high-precision laser to melt and fuse materials together. Friction stir welding uses a rotating tool to stir the metals together, and that friction generates enough heat to soften the materials. JOINS will perform these welding approaches on two different materials: aluminum and stainless-steel. Credit: Lockheed Martin

will mature technologies that allow robotic systems to join materials directly in space. In-space joining could enable large structures to be assembled and integrated after launch rather than being constrained by the size and volume of a launch vehicle. Testing technologies in space helps validate their performance in unique environmental conditions, matures their readiness for operational use, reduces technical risk, and builds confidence for future mission applications.
Additional supplies being flown to the space station include:

li: Crew quarter blankets and covers to replace old units on station.
Hatch seal covers to be installed on U.S. segment hatch seals.
A modified toilet pretreat hose needed to operate the universal pretreat concentrate tank in the Universal Waste Management System toilet.
Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer specific spacewalk tools to be used during upcoming spacewalks.
Anomaly Gas Analyzer batteries required to power various sensors on space station.
